newsitem.title: UKRAINE: UKRAINE, POLAND SIGN HISTORIC RECONCILIATION PACT.
newsitem.headline: UKRAINE, POLAND SIGN HISTORIC RECONCILIATION PACT.

text.p: The presidents of Ukraine and Poland proclaimed on Wednesday that they had put centuries of bloodshed behind them in the latest move towards reconciliation between once-warring European neighbours.
Ukraine's Leonid Kuchma and Poland's Alexander Kwasniewski signed a Declaration on Accord and Unity aimed at ending conflict and mistrust between the neighbouring Slav nations.

"Germans and French, Germans and Czechs, Germans and Poles, Hungarians and Romanians have been reconciled despite all the difficult events in history, the non-tolerance and wars in the past," Kwasniewski said.

"We have a unique opportunity and we have no right to miss it...The past should not be repeated in the future," he said after a signing ceremony watched by hundreds of students at Kiev's elite Institute for International Relations.
Ukrainian cossacks fought Polish troops in the 17th and 18th centuries in what they saw as a struggle for an independent Ukraine and against Catholicism on Orthodox soil.

But the most painful memory clouding relations is the killing of 34,650 Poles by nationalist insurgents in western Ukraine in 1942-1943 and the forced resettlement of more than 150,000 Ukrainians from one part of Poland to another in 1947.
"If blood was spilled in the past there is a need to tell of it...We understand it by forgiving and asking forgiveness," Kuchma said.
Each state views the other as a strategic partner and Warsaw sees the presence of a stable and independent Ukraine as a buffer next to Russia as good for its security.

Unlike Russia, Ukraine supports Poland's bid to join the NATO defence alliance but has not applied for membership itself, though it is seeking security guarantees. Poland has promoted Kiev's integration into European structures.
Both Kuchma and Kwasniewski rejected Moscow's insistence that NATO admit new members only among former Soviet satellites but never among former Soviet republics.
"Russia has no veto right on the ability of sovereign states to carry out their sovereign foreign policy," said Kwasniewski. "This is how Europe differs from what it was several years ago."
Ukraine is due to take another step towards reconciliation with its neighbours when Russian President Boris Yeltsin visits Kiev on May 30-31 to sign a political treaty.
Relations between Ukraine and Russia have been uneasy since the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
They have been overshadowed by the division of the Black Sea fleet and Soviet assets and Ukrainian suspicions that Russia harbours imperialist ambitions.

Kuchma is also due to sign a friendship and cooperation treaty with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu on June 2 after three years of talks dogged by differences over lands Romania lost to the Soviet Union before World War Two.
